actionThatDiffers: At 88% with 40 minutes to reset, the user does not kick off the 90-minute refactor; they ask the running session for a handoff summary first.
argument: Placed outside; I tried to move it inside and could not. But 12 is too low: 12 means a harness puts it on screen unprompted, which is only true for the minority who installed a third-party status line like Barista. The briefing's baseline user runs no custom monitoring, so the honest route is `/usage` — one command, in a place the user knows to look, i.e. 21-40. The account-level 5h window is a single global number, so one call answers it for the whole fleet; there is nothing to correlate, which is why no fleet argument rescues it. Impact survives rule 1 with a concrete action, but 88 overstates it: the raw percentage plus reset time is a readout, and the author himself argues the decision only appears once A5 projects it. 82.

actionThatDiffers: Thursday, weekly window at 90%: defer the multi-day migration to Monday, or drop to Sonnet for the rest of the week.
argument: Same source and same command as A1, so access is 28, not 18 — one command, not on screen unprompted. The real attack is on impact. Rule 1: name the action. The weekly-window action is 'don't start a big one', which is soft, deferrable and reversible — people start anyway and absorb the wait — and it presents itself roughly once a week rather than several times a day. Compare A1 and A3, where the remedy is immediate and cheap (wait 40 minutes, or switch model). A number whose decision surfaces weekly, whose remedy is 'plan differently', and which is one keystroke away belongs in 51-75, near the bottom: 58. Its 70 came from riding A1's coat-tails rather than from its own delta.

actionThatDiffers: Opus sub-limit nearly gone but Sonnet untouched: type /model sonnet and keep working instead of stalling two hours.
argument: Correct as placed, and the best-scored item in the quota cluster. Access stays at 38: the per-model breakdown arrives in the same authenticated payload the harness already renders in `/usage`, so it is one command away, but it is one step deeper in that output than the aggregate and only exists on plans that have sub-limits, which justifies the top of the 21-40 band rather than the bottom. No promotion into the differentiated quadrant is available: nothing here requires correlating across sessions or across time. Impact trimmed 76 to 72 only because the remedy presupposes the work tolerates a weaker model, which is a judgement the user still has to make. The action is genuinely concrete and cheap, which is what keeps it above A2.

actionThatDiffers: Answer the blocking prompt three minutes after it appears rather than twenty-five, so twelve idle agent-minutes are not spent per gate.
argument: The closest call on the board, and I could not honestly push it inside. The strongest inside argument is that a pane sweep is a snapshot while the value is continuous timeliness — but that is an argument about polling frequency, not about access, and rule 2 forecloses it: `tmux list-panes` plus `capture-pane` piped through a grep for the prompt glyph gives an adequate approximation of 'which of my twelve is waiting' in one pass. Approximate-but-good-enough counts as reachable, so access is capped at 60. I hold it at 58 rather than lower because the judgement step is real (a blocked pane and a thinking pane both end in text you have to read) and because sessions living in separate iTerm tabs or windows fall outside tmux entirely. Impact stands at 88 under rule 6: shipped, but the loss it prevents is concrete and recurring.

actionThatDiffers: None. The same answer gets typed; only the window it is typed into changes.
argument: Placed at 78/35, i.e. outside on access already — the attack is on impact, and it is the cleanest kill on this list. Rule 5: this is something the user DOES, so access is how hard it is to do today, and switching to a tab and typing a reply is 21-40. The author has that right. Rule 1 then decides it: I cannot name any action that differs between having and not having this. The prompt gets the same answer, the session proceeds identically, and the only saving is the trip. That is the textbook 'minor convenience' band, so impact is 40, not 78. 78 was measuring how much the trip annoys the user, which is frustration, not delta. This matters more than the number: at 78 it is the highest-impact item still unbuilt and it drags DEC-2 forward with it; at 40 it is a 92-build convenience and DEC-2 loses its loudest justification.

actionThatDiffers: The tracked plan says 'add retry to the uploader' and the diff also rewrites the auth middleware: stop the session and re-scope before the branch becomes unreviewable.
argument: Placed outside, and it should move toward the quadrant without reaching it — the author's stated reason for the drop is contaminated. The note says the score fell because a local model or a third promise amendment is needed. That is build cost, landing in impact this time rather than in access: the same leak he corrected on the x-axis, mirrored. Judged on delta alone the action is concrete and expensive to miss, but it overlaps C2, C5 and C3, and the same catch usually arrives from a cheaper detector, so 58, not 48 and not 70. Access comes down from 80 to 70: for any one session the plan and `git diff` are both a keystroke away, and rule 2's sweep gets you the dirty files per pane; what stays out of reach is the cross-session, over-time comparison and the semantic judgement. Rule 4 applies — nothing computes this, so the value rests on the matcher being right, and a matcher that cries drift on a legitimate refactor is worse than silence.

actionThatDiffers: Two sessions in the same worktree: move one into a git worktree, or hold the second until the first lands, instead of discovering a clobbered file later.
argument: Placed at 70/55, outside; I attacked toward inside and it collapses under two rules at once. Rule 2: the sweep answers this directly — `tmux list-panes -a -F '#{pane_current_path}'` is one line and yields every session's directory. Rule 3: the transform on top is a duplicate check over a set, pure arithmetic over inputs that are individually visible, so the cap is 60 and the honest figure is 45. This is the item on the list furthest from a moat, and the author half-admits it ('the failure is attention rather than access') while still scoring it at 55. Impact trims to 66: the collision is expensive when it happens, but the user chooses the directory each time they start a session, so this is a lapse they can also prevent by looking. It stays worth building on a build cost of 10, which is a different argument from differentiation.

actionThatDiffers: Nothing reliable. The user already knows which repo is production; a stakes field only reorders a list they can already read.
argument: Correct as placed at 38/25, and I could not build an inside case worth writing. Access is genuinely low for an unusual reason: the information is not in a tool, it is in the user's head. They know which of their repos deploys to production and which is a scratch clone, and no lookup is required to retrieve it, so this is below the 21-40 band, not above it. That is the opposite of the E4 shape, where the user has forgotten the session existed. Impact holds at 38 because the honest version must be inferred, rule 4 applies, and a wrong inference is actively harmful: the user reorders their attention around a label that is confidently wrong. The author reached this by agreeing with CL rather than by argument, but the placement survives scrutiny anyway.

actionThatDiffers: Commit or stash the dirty worktree from the session that died at 6pm, instead of losing it to the next branch switch, machine reboot, or agent that reuses the directory.
argument: Confirming the earlier audit and hardening it. 50 prices the route as 'cd there and run git status', which assumes the user remembers the session existed — and the defining property of this item is that they do not. The real route is: enumerate sessions that have already ended (nothing displays these; you would be listing transcript directories under the harness's store by hand), map each to its working directory, then run git status in every one, then decide which dirt is stale versus fresh. That is correlating across time in a way most people will not do reliably: 61-80. It is also the one class rule 2 cannot touch, and that is the general lesson — an ended session has no pane and no process, so the sweep that answers B1, C8 and G2 returns nothing at all. Impact holds at 80: the loss is concrete work already paid for. This lands inside the differentiated quadrant at 80/70.

actionThatDiffers: The user runs the commission flow they can already run, with the session list pre-filled instead of described by hand.
argument: Placed at 80/55 in the contested zone; both numbers are wrong in the same direction. Rule 5 first: promoting a session to a workflow is something the user DOES, so access is how hard it is to do today — invoke the existing commission workflow and answer its questions. That is one prompt, 21-40, not 55. Then rule 1: the differing action is not 'the FO takes over versus you orchestrate', because the user can already commission a workflow whenever they decide to; the difference is that the setup is pre-populated from observed sessions. Saved setup time is real but it is convenience, so 50. Note the internal inconsistency the author left standing: F6 needs everything B4 needs and more, he marked B4 down explicitly for being keystroke-saving, and then left F6 at 80 on the strength of a positioning argument. Positioning is not impact, by his own rule.

actionThatDiffers: None. A rate with no ceiling supports no threshold, so nothing is done differently after looking at it.
argument: Correct as placed, and useful precisely because it is. Access stays high: no harness prints tokens-per-minute, and reconstructing a time series means parsing transcript records, so 61-80 — I take 65 rather than 70 because the underlying counts are partly visible via the status line and `/context`, which makes the very roughest version eyeballable. Impact stays at 24 under rule 1: I cannot name an action, and rule 6 does not spare it for being shipped and attractive. This is the board's honest calibration point for the hard-and-worthless quadrant, and pulling it toward the middle to flatter shipped work would cost more than it gains.

actionThatDiffers: None. A count with no verb after it.
argument: Correct as placed at 20/20, and both rules that could move it push it in the direction the author already chose. Rule 3: a count is the purest arithmetic composite over individually visible inputs, so it is capped at 60 and in fact sits far lower — rule 2's sweep answers it with `tmux list-panes -a | wc -l`, and the user usually knows the number from having opened the tabs. Rule 1 gives no action at all. No attack available in either direction; the only thing worth saying is that the item earns its place by populating the low-impact, low-access corner honestly.

actionThatDiffers: None. Streaks and weekly counts are for looking at.
argument: Impact 14 is right and I leave it. Access 75 is wrong, and the error is instructive: the author reasoned from 'no harness retains queryable history' straight to 'effectively unobtainable', which is the nonexistent-versus-withheld confusion pointed the wrong way. History is not absent — the harness leaves a transcript file per session on disk, with timestamps. 'Sessions this week' is a `find` over the store plus `wc -l`; a streak is the same list with dates deduped. That is one command a competent developer would actually run, plus some manual work to make it presentable, so 41-60, and I take 48. Rule 4 does not apply because nothing has to be inferred; the data is sitting there. This also disciplines its neighbours: H1's premise is retention and querying, not the existence of the raw record.

actionThatDiffers: After seeing a force-push logged in an auto-approved session, recover from the reflog inside the window, and turn auto-approve off for that session.
argument: Placed at 55/72, outside; the honest move is further out. Access first: the author's own rewrite concedes this is a log of what already happened, and what already happened is written down in three places the user can reach — the session's own scrollback, the transcript on disk (one grep for `push --force`, `rm -rf`, `DROP`), and for git specifically the reflog itself. Rule 2's sweep gets the live half; a grep over the transcript store gets the historical half. That is several places and some manual work, so 58, not 76-plus. Impact 50, not 55: the recovery action is real but rare, and the same window is already covered by git's own safety nets and by the harness permission prompts everywhere except the auto-approved sessions the author correctly identifies as the whole remaining value. Rule 4 flags the dangerous-command matcher: too narrow and it misses, too broad and it becomes another ignored log.

actionThatDiffers: Claude at 95% and Codex at 10%: restate the task in Codex and keep going, instead of waiting out the reset.
argument: Correct as placed, and the author's self-correction from 72 to 50 was right for the right reason. Rule 3 nails it: for the two harnesses in the worked example both inputs are individually visible — Claude's `/usage` and Codex's native TUI usage line — and the transform is a max over two numbers, so the cap is 60. I nudge to 55 rather than 50 because the briefing says quota display is absent on most of the other harnesses, so the inputs stop being visible as the fleet widens; that keeps it mid-scale but not low. Impact down from 79 to 70: the remedy is not a keystroke like A3's, it is re-establishing context in a different harness with none of the session state carried over, so the action does not reliably follow from the information. Real, regular, and short of the 76-100 band.

actionThatDiffers: Pause the one session that has eaten 60% of the window rather than stopping all four, or stopping nothing and guessing.
argument: Placed outside on impact at 66/76, and it stays outside — but not where the author put it. Access down to 68: the briefing confirms no harness attributes consumption to a session, so cumulative share really does require correlating across sessions and across time, which keeps it in 61-80. It does not deserve 76, because rule 2's sweep yields a serviceable approximation — the user can usually see which pane is grinding a 200-file refactor and which is answering a question — and approximate-but-good-enough counts. Impact down to 62: the guess the sweep produces is usually correct, so the delta is being right when the intuition is wrong rather than knowing at all, and the remedy costs whatever that session had in flight. Note that stripping A1 from it leaves A10, which the board already scores at 62 with a build of 12; A7 is A10 plus a denominator, and the denominator is not worth 14 points of impact.
